The words

Our heavenly Father calls,
And Christ invites us near;
With both my friendship shall be sweet,
And my communion dear.

God pities all my griefs;
He pardons every day;
Almighty to protect my soul,
And wise to guide my way.

Jesus, my living Head,
I bless thy faithful care;
My Advocate before the throne,
And my Forerunner there.

Here fix my roving heart;
Here wait my warmest love,
Till the communion be complete,
In nobler scenes above.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum Eb and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on d (E♭), on the word “Our”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

Philip Doddridge wrote these words. They were printed in Hymns for Christian Devotion, compiled by John G. Adams and Edwin H. Chapin (Boston, 1846), as hymn 686 of its twenty-second edition (1853), “Communion with God and Christ”.

The book printed the words without tunes, marked Short Metre (6.6.8.6), to be sung to any tune of that metre. This page sets them to FRANCONIA; any other Short Metre tune fits them as well.

  • Words: Philip Doddridge (1702–1751)
  • Music (1738): Johann Balthasar König (1691–1758)

Questions about Our Heavenly Father Calls

What is the doh of Our Heavenly Father Calls?

In this version, in Eb major, doh is Eb. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Our Heavenly Father Calls start on?

It starts on d (E♭ in Eb major), a pickup on the word “Our” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to d.

Is Our Heavenly Father Calls in the public domain?

Yes. Philip Doddridge died in 1751, Johann Balthasar König died in 1758; the words were in print by 1853 and the music in 1738. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
